sm: Albert Mohler speaks from Washington, D.C., about a week after the midterm elections, as orientation for new members of Congress begins. He cites a Financial Times analysis naming three trends: a younger, richer, more diverse new South, a resurgence of an old left of union and working voters, and a prairie populism in places like Iowa and Kansas that turned against tariffs and the Iran war. He says Texas is the striking case, where every statewide office was Republican until now and only Senator Ted Cruz remains, with James Talarico winning John Cornyn's Senate seat. He argues the left's return may reflect frustration with President Trump and tariffs rather than a lasting shift, and that higher prices burden consumers.

Mohler says that if Republicans abandon the blue collar voters who joined the party since 1980, those voters will leave, and he calls the left's victory larger the longer he looks at it. He turns to congressional leadership, noting Republicans are now in the minority in both houses. House Republicans chose Jim Jordan as minority leader over Steve Scalise in a secret ballot, which he says signals a scrappier, more aggressive minority. Senate Republicans re-elected John Thune of South Dakota as their leader, which he says shows the Senate charting its own course apart from President Trump. He then notes a Washington Post headline about growing opposition to Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries leading the Democrats.

Mohler says the most interesting worldview collision now is within the Democratic Party. Schumer is celebrated by some Democrats and loathed by others, partly because several Senate nominees were not his choices, and those new senators will help decide whether he stays leader. He predicts Hakeem Jeffries will become Speaker, noting he would be the first African-American Speaker, even though some Democrats want to move further left. He mentions Elizabeth Warren becoming Senate Banking Committee chair. He discusses reports that between nine and thirteen democratic socialists were elected, a Washington Post editorial titled MBAs versus DSA saying socialists should stay on the fringes, and a New York Times headline about progressives still facing electability questions.

Mohler says California voters defeated a one-time billionaire wealth tax, but he expects the left, including Bernie Sanders, to push for a national wealth tax, which he says raises constitutional questions. He then discusses a New York Times article headlined that Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has evolved and wants the left to evolve too, and he expects her to seek the 2028 Democratic nomination. He objects to the evolution language from a biblical perspective and notes the article itself recalls her past left-wing positions, including the Green New Deal and her defund the police remarks. He closes by saying Christians should care about these events without treating them as ultimate, and should keep a biblical balance.
